title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.
key_points: A classical bit is 0 or 1; a qubit can be in a superposition of both until measured.
Entangling qubits links their fates, letting them represent many combinations at once.
For specific problems — code-breaking, simulating molecules — this could vastly outpace normal computers.
Qubits are fragile: the tiniest disturbance collapses them, so they need extreme isolation.
content_html: An ordinary computer stores information in bits, each firmly a 0 or a 1. A quantum computer uses qubits, which exploit the strange rules of quantum physics. Thanks to superposition, a qubit isn't pinned to 0 or 1 but can hold a blend of both possibilities at once, committing to a definite value only when you measure it. On its own that's curious; the real power comes when qubits are entangled, their states linked so that a group of them can represent an enormous number of combinations simultaneously.
extra_html: This doesn't make quantum computers simply "faster" at everything — for most everyday tasks they offer no advantage. But for a special class of problems they could be transformative: factoring huge numbers (which would upend today's encryption), simulating molecules and materials for chemistry and drug design, and certain search and optimization tasks. The enormous obstacle is fragility. A qubit's quantum state is destroyed by the faintest stray interaction with its surroundings — a process called decoherence — so real machines must isolate their qubits and keep them frigid, while juggling elaborate error correction. Today's quantum computers are still small and error-prone, more promising laboratory than finished tool. Wikipedia surveys the principles, the algorithms, and where the technology stands.

related.title: What Makes Quantum Physics Weird
related.hook: In the quantum world energy comes in lumps, particles act like waves, and you can't pin down everything at once — and yet it's our best-tested theory.

related.title: Quantum Entanglement
related.hook: Two particles can share one quantum state so tightly that measuring one instantly fixes the other's matching property — even light-years apart. Einstein called it spooky.

related.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
related.hook: Nature sets a hard limit: the more precisely you know where a particle is, the less you can know about how it's moving. It's not sloppy measurement — it's built into reality.

related.title: Tiny Magnetic Waves Could Shrink Quantum Computers to Coin Size
related.hook: Magnons — quantum ripples of magnetism once too short-lived to use — just got a 100x lifespan boost, and the bottleneck turns out to be manufacturing, not physics.

flashcards.prompt: How does a qubit differ from a classical bit?
flashcards.back_html: A bit is strictly 0 or 1. A qubit can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1 at the same time, settling on one value only when measured.

flashcards.prompt: What lets a quantum computer tackle certain problems classical ones can't?

choices.text: Superposition and entanglement let many qubits represent vast combinations at once
It runs many ordinary computers side by side

flashcards.explanation_html: By putting qubits in superposition and entangling them, a quantum computer processes a huge space of possibilities together — for specific tasks, not all.

flashcards.prompt: Why are quantum computers so hard to build?

choices.text: Qubits are extremely fragile — the slightest disturbance collapses their quantum state
They require more electricity than exists
Quantum effects only work above room temperature

flashcards.explanation_html: Almost any stray interaction with the environment destroys a qubit's superposition (decoherence), so they must be isolated and error-corrected.
